analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic refuge's coastal plain to oil drilling, with royalties funding heating aid, weatherization, and infant nutrition programs.
analysis.headline: The bill would have opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas leasing, but it was referred to committee on the day it was introduced in March 2008 and never received a hearing or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the ban on oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and required the Interior Department to hold competitive lease sales on its coastal plain, with the first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months. It included environmental conditions—a 2,000-acre cap on the development footprint, seasonal protections for caribou calving, and rules meant to prevent significant harm to fish, wildlife, and subsistence hunting—but also shortcut the usual review process by barring study of a no-leasing alternative and limiting court challenges. Money from the leases would have been split between alternative energy programs and aid for low-income households: heating assistance, home weatherization, and the WIC nutrition program. The bill took effect only if oil prices averaged $125 a barrel or more for five consecutive days.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, oil and gas companies would gain access to leases in a currently off-limits part of the Arctic refuge, paying at least a 12.5% royalty plus cash bonus bids. Alaska Native corporations would receive land conveyances and hiring and contracting preferences. Low-income households would benefit from the revenue stream: half of lease receipts to federal alternative energy programs, and roughly a sixth each to home heating assistance (LIHEAP), home weatherization, and the WIC nutrition program. North Slope communities would get $35 million a year in impact aid, and unionized construction workers would gain from required project labor agreements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, Alaska Native corporations, low-income energy users

how_it_helps.text: Half of all leasing revenue would go to Department of Energy alternative energy programs, and one-sixth each to low-income home energy assistance (LIHEAP), the Weatherization Assistance Program for low-income households, and the WIC nutrition program for women, infants, and children.

$35 million a year would go into a fund for North Slope communities—covering firefighting, police, water treatment, and first-responder services—and to compensate residents for damage to subsistence and cultural resources.
Oil produced under the leases could not be exported, keeping it in the domestic market.

Leases would require companies to negotiate project labor agreements with building-trades unions and to use best efforts to provide a fair share of jobs and contracts to Alaska Natives and Alaska Native corporations.

The bill sets a 2,000-acre cap on the total surface footprint of production facilities, requires seasonal closures to protect caribou calving areas, and mandates a 'no significant adverse effect' standard for fish, wildlife, and subsistence resources.

analysis.who_pays: The public would give up permanent protection of the refuge's coastal plain, trading an undisturbed Arctic ecosystem and subsistence hunting grounds for industrial development. The bill's own design would narrow the public's ability to fight that development in court, and any new oil would take years to reach market with no guaranteed effect on prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public; the untouched Arctic refuge

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the legal prohibition on oil and gas production in the Arctic refuge and declares leasing 'compatible' with the refuge's purposes, with no further findings required—opening a currently protected wilderness area to industrial development.

It shortcuts environmental review: the Interior Secretary would not have to study the alternative of not leasing at all, and public comments on the draft environmental study would be accepted for only 20 days.

Court challenges would be funneled to a single court (the D.C. Circuit) with a 90-day filing deadline, and the government's environmental analysis would be presumed correct unless disproven by 'clear and convincing' evidence—a high bar for opponents.
The bill only takes effect once oil averages $125 a barrel or more for five straight days, meaning it activates precisely when prices—and industry's incentive to drill—are at their highest.
The funding for heating aid, weatherization, and nutrition programs depends entirely on drilling revenue, so those benefits arrive only if the refuge is developed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was designed as a bargain: open a protected Arctic refuge to drilling, and dedicate the money to things many people support—heating aid, weatherization, infant nutrition, and alternative energy—while imposing real conditions on drillers (12.5% royalties, a 2,000-acre surface footprint, seasonal limits, a domestic-only sales requirement, and labor agreements). The serious costs are on the other side of the ledger: the development would be effectively permanent, the environmental review is deliberately narrow (no non-drilling alternative examined, a 20-day comment window), and the courts would be instructed to presume the Interior Department correct unless proven wrong by clear and convincing evidence—so if the protections fell short, the public's tools to challenge that would be few. And the bill takes effect only when oil is expensive, when the pressure to extract is greatest. Whether the mitigation genuinely suffices is the core honest dispute; the shortcuts in review and court access tilt the design toward the lessees.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or floor time before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lisa Murkowski introduced S. 2758 on March 13, 2008; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The action history shows no further steps—no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action—before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
Because bills die when a Congress ends, the measure would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Arctic refuge stayed closed to drilling and oil companies gained no new leases there; conservation interests got the outcome they wanted by default. The flip side is that the bill's promised funding for heating aid, weatherization, and WIC never materialized either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Conservation interests; oil companies lost lease access

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas leasing.

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Joined Murkowski in introducing the bill ('for herself and Mr. Stevens').

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote—so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: National environmental and conservation groups
against.role: Advocacy organizations opposing Arctic refuge drilling
against.what_they_did: Opposed opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil development, a position they pressed throughout the decade's repeated ANWR drilling fights.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and five of the seven cosponsors were Republicans, with two Democrats also signing on, but no vote ever occurred to reveal where the Senate stood.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to give oil companies access to leases in the Arctic refuge's coastal plain, at a 12.5% royalty, with a first sale of at least 200,000 acres required within 22 months. The public would receive royalty revenue earmarked for energy aid and other programs, but the underlying resource is public land and the development would be effectively permanent.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation, Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill conveys surface and subsurface land to these corporations, encourages Native hiring and contracting on the leases, and funds community impact aid in the affected villages.

industries.industry: Conservation, wilderness, and subsistence users of the Arctic refuge
industries.note: The coastal plain would shift from protected wilderness to an active leasing program, ending the current prohibition on production. Local subsistence hunting and fishing would face new restrictions and development pressure.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and low-income energy assistance programs
industries.note: Half the leasing revenue would fund Department of Energy alternative energy programs under 2005 and 2007 energy laws, creating a new dedicated funding stream—but only if drilling proceeds.
